Enzyme 3D Lab

Every second, your cells make a poison — hydrogen peroxide — and an enzyme called catalase destroys it almost instantly. Run the classic catalase foam experiment on a 3D lab bench, then zoom down to a single enzyme to see why temperature, pH and inhibitors change how fast it works. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

⚗️ The reaction

2 H₂O₂ —catalase→ 2 H₂O + O₂

Hydrogen peroxide is the substrate. Water and oxygen are the products. The enzyme is not used up — one catalase molecule can break down millions of H₂O₂ molecules every second.

🔑 The big idea

shape → function

An enzyme works only while its active site has the right shape. Heat, the wrong pH and inhibitors all slow it down by changing or blocking that shape.

3D lab furniture and equipment (cabinets, lab bottles, vials, clock, stools, safety glasses, sink, first-aid cabinet, extinguisher, SDS binder, steel table, cutting board, kettle, scalpel, spatula, dissecting tray): NVIDIA SimReady assets, licensed under CC BY 4.0; converted from OpenUSD and simplified for offline use. Water bath, glassware, tissue, enzyme, molecules and all simulations: © Digital Vector · digitalvector.com.au. Model numbers are simplified for teaching and are not real measurements.

Teacher notes

Two self-contained labs in one offline HTML file. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks included). Nothing is uploaded; results are saved in the browser on that device only, and students can download their data as a CSV.

Suggested sequence (2 class periods)

  • Lab 1 (1 period): controlled experiment. Pick one independent variable (temperature, pH, H₂O₂ concentration, amount of tissue or surface area), keep the rest constant, run three trials per level and graph the means. The dependent variable is foam volume after 60 seconds (reading − 10 mL of liquid). Students can read the cylinder themselves; wrong readings are corrected.
  • Lab 2 (½–1 period): collision theory, active site, induced fit vs lock and key, denaturation, pH, competitive vs non-competitive inhibition, activation energy, and real enzymes with different optimums.

What the models assume

  • Lab 1: catalase activity doubles for every 10 °C rise up to 37 °C, then falls; tissue warmed above about 40 °C for 5 minutes loses activity that does not come back (boiled tissue makes no foam). pH optimum is about 7. Rate rises with H₂O₂ concentration but levels off (saturation). Liver has far more catalase than potato; apple very little. Chopping or mashing exposes more cells. Each trial varies a little, like real tissue.
  • Lab 2 is not to scale: real catalase is a huge four-part protein, and one molecule can break down millions of H₂O₂ molecules per second. The animation is slowed so students can see each event.
  • All numbers are simplified for teaching. They show the right patterns, not real measurements.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-PS1-5 (effect of temperature and concentration on reaction rate), HS-LS1-1 (proteins carry out the work of cells), HS-LS1-3 (feedback and homeostasis — why body temperature and pH are kept stable). Practices: planning and carrying out investigations; analyzing and interpreting data; developing and using models.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42): B.11B (investigate and explain the role of enzymes in facilitating cellular processes).
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.3 (follow a multistep experimental procedure, taking measurements); RST.9-10.7 (translate between words, tables and graphs).
  • AP Biology: Unit 3 Cellular Energetics — 3.1 Enzyme Structure, 3.2 Enzyme Catalysis, 3.3 Environmental Impacts on Enzyme Function.

If you also run the wet lab

  • 3% hydrogen peroxide is the pharmacy strength — still wear goggles and gloves. Use fresh liver or potato, a water bath rather than a flame, and dispose of tissue in the trash, not the sink.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan. Gray buttons explain why they cannot be used yet when you tap them.
